bio: A Basran hadith narrator (kunya Abu al-Nadr) regarded as trustworthy (thiqah), though he experienced ikhtilat (confusion) late in life and his son prevented him from narrating during that period. He was considered particularly weak in narrations from Qatadah and made errors when narrating from memory, yet was respected as a memorizer. His narrations appear in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
research_evidence: ت. ١٧٠ هـ (died 170 AH)

bio: A Kufan hadith narrator and judge, born near the end of Uthman's caliphate, described as among the most eloquent of people. His memory deteriorated before his death and he was known for tadlis (concealing narration sources); scholars disagreed on his reliability — some rated him trustworthy while others criticized his inconsistencies. Around 200 of his hadith transmissions are recorded.

bio: An Egyptian hadith scholar and historian of Yemeni family origin who became the first judge of Egypt appointed directly by a caliph, serving as qadi from 772 to 780 under al-Mansur with a salary of 30 dinars per month. His library burned in a fire in 786. Later hadith scholars criticized him for omissions in his chains of transmission.
research_evidence: He died in the year 790. (174 AH)

bio: Musa ibn Uqba was a freedman of the al-Zubayr family in Medina and studied under al-Zuhri and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr. He composed the Kitab al-Maghazi, one of the earliest works on the Prophet's military campaigns, lost for centuries and rediscovered in 2021 at Tunisia's National Library. His work was praised by scholars including Malik ibn Anas and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
research_evidence: The majority of scholars recorded Mūsa's death as having occurred in 141 AH / 758–759 CE in Medina.

bio: Zayd ibn al-Hubab was a Kufan hadith scholar of Khurasani origin and a freedman of the Uqayl tribe. He traveled extensively seeking knowledge, visiting Iraq, Syria, the Hijaz, Egypt, and al-Andalus. He was considered a trustworthy transmitter despite some criticism of occasional errors in memory-based narrations, and his narrations appear in five of the six canonical hadith collections (excluding Sahih al-Bukhari).
research_evidence: 203/819 ... Zilhicce ayinda (Haziran 819) [died in the month of Dhul-Hijjah 203 AH / June 819 CE]

bio: Born in Kufa and raised in Basra, he was counted among the leading Basran advocates of the Sunna. He said he never wrote anything down, relying entirely on memory, and was famed for scrupulous honesty in trade — once returning profit to a buyer after discovering a cloak he sold was underpriced. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ibn Ma'in held him trustworthy, though al-Nasa'i and others flagged him for tadlis.

bio: A meticulous Kufan transmitter who reportedly listened to a tradition three times before accepting it and would not narrate to anyone until first asking whether they followed the Sunnah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal counted him among the four greatest hadith scholars alongside Sufyan, Shu'ba, and Zuhayr. He died in Byzantine territory during al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba's summer campaign.

He was regarded as reliable overall, though his transmission from Ikrima was considered confused and he was noted as prone to accepting prompting when questioned.

bio: A Kufan hadith master who moved to the Jazira region around 164 AH and became known as its muhaddith. He was praised for precision — one saying held that 'Zuhayr is more precise than twenty like Shu'ba' — and Ahmad ibn Hanbal counted him among the 'mines of knowledge'. He suffered a stroke about a year before his death, but his retention was said to be unaffected.

bio: Basran in origin, he settled in al-Yamama in central Arabia. Scholars disagreed on his reliability: some graded him trustworthy (thiqa), while his narrations from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir in particular were criticized as confused. He was said to be illiterate but of excellent memory.

His memory declined in his final years, and scholars debated whether he underwent full ikhtilat (confusion); several other transmitters bore the identical name, distinguished only by tribal nisba.

bio: A Medinan jurist and hadith scholar whom Sufyan al-Thawri called 'commander of the faithful in hadith'; about 300 students are said to have attended his circle at once. He died suddenly in his washing chamber on a Friday night in Ramadan at age 66, and had a known rivalry with the jurist Rabi'a.

bio: The leading hadith transmitter of Homs in Syria, born 108 AH (102, 105, and 106 also reported). Scholars considered him highly reliable in transmitting from Syrian narrators but criticized his reports from Hijazi and Iraqi transmitters, attributed to lost manuscripts and reliance on memory. He is said to have inherited 4,000 dinars from his father and spent it all on seeking knowledge.

bio: A Kufan scholar who transmitted the Qira'at of 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud through Shu'bah after some forty years of study. He was a non-sectarian legal scholar who opposed both the Hanafi and Maliki schools of his time. His surviving book Kitab al-Kharaj is regarded as a foundational work of traditionalist economic thought.
research_evidence: Yahya ibn Adam died as a stranger in Famm al-Silah during mid-Rabi' al-Awwal 203 AH (mid-September 818 CE)

bio: A Meccan hadith transmitter of al-Qara, an ally of Banu Zuhra, with the kunya Abu 'Uthman. Classical critics differed on him: al-'Ijli called him trustworthy (thiqa) and Ibn Abi Hatim's father found him acceptable and sound in hadith, while Yahya ibn Ma'in said his reports are not strong and it was noted that he made errors. Sources differ on his death year, giving 132 AH, 135 AH, or before 144 AH.
research_evidence: سنة اثْنَتَيْنِ وَثَلَاثِينَ وَمِائَة (132 AH); other reports on the page give 135 AH or before 144 AH

bio: Born in Abyssinia around 622 or 626 CE during his parents' emigration; nephew of Ali and husband of Zaynab bint Ali. He was called 'Bahr al-Jud' (ocean of generosity) and was among Medina's richest men, renowned for philanthropy. Two of his sons, Awn and Muhammad, were killed at Karbala, which he missed due to poor eyesight. The page gives his death as c. 699, with 702/704 as alternative dates.
classif: Military commander at the Battle of Siffin

bio: A Medinan historian who specialized in the maghazi genre, the military campaigns of Muhammad. His books on the early Islamic expeditions and conquests predate much of the later Abbasid-period Sunni and Shia literature. Later hadith scholars extensively criticized his reliability as a hadith transmitter.
notable_works: Kitab al-Tarikh wa al-Maghazi (Book of History and Campaigns)
a book on the death of Husayn ibn Ali (not survived)
a book on Muhammad's last days (not survived)

He fought in the naval battle of Dhat al-Sawari, where he lost an eye, enjoyed the favor of the governor Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, and spent his final years with the garrison in North Africa. His name was reportedly said as the diminutive 'Ulayy' because of Umayyad hostility to the name Ali.

bio: A Kufan transmitter of Ju'f said to have been born in the Year of the Elephant, who arrived in Medina just after the Prophet's death and narrated from the earliest caliphs. His humility was legendary: when offered high positions he declined, saying his bread and salt sufficed him.

Ahmad estimated he had about fifty hadiths in circulation.

Ibn Hajar classified him as reliable with some unique narrations ('thiqa lahu afrad'), and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said he was firmly established with all his teachers. He held predestinarian (Qadari) views but did not speak of them publicly; al-Hakim, Ibn Khuzayma and Abu 'Awana included his narrations in their collections.
research_evidence: في حدود 160 هـ (died around 160 AH)

bio: A Basran hadith master nicknamed 'Arim, counted among the most reliable students of Hammad ibn Zayd after 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi. His memory deteriorated in his final years, with confusion pronounced around 216 AH, so narrations taken from him before the decline are considered sound while later ones require verification. Al-Bukhari and Ahmad ibn Hanbal were among those who transmitted from him.
research_evidence: مَاتَ عَارمٌ سَنَةَ أَرْبَعٍ وَعِشْرِيْنَ فِي صَفَرٍ (Arim died in Safar of the year [two hundred and] twenty-four)

bio: An Egyptian hadith narrator regarded as both reliable and exceptionally pious: al-Hakim called him 'thiqa ma'mun', Ibn Hibban listed him among reliable narrators, and Ibn Hajar graded him 'thiqa 'abid' (trustworthy and devout), placing him in the seventh generation per al-Taqrib. He was described as 'among the best of Muhammad's community'.
research_evidence: Death year: 168هـ (168 AH)

bio: A Damascene traditionist known as al-Makhuli for his association with Makhul. 'Abd al-Razzaq said he never saw anyone more scrupulous in hadith than him. Scholars disagreed on his reliability — Ahmad ibn Hanbal declared him trustworthy while al-Nasa'i judged him 'not strong' — and sources note he held Qadarite views and possibly Shi'ite leanings, which made some reluctant to transmit from him.

bio: A Basran teacher who settled in Mecca, known by the kunya Abu Umayya. Hadith critics unanimously considered him weak ('mujma' 'ala da'fihi'); Ibn Hajar rated him da'if, and his Murji'ite views were also noted, though some accepted his reports in non-legal matters. Malik ibn Anas, Shu'ba and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna nevertheless transmitted from him.
research_evidence: Death year: 126 or 127 AH (page's death-date field)

bio: A Basran scholar and famed ascetic who took part in military campaigns beyond the Euphrates under Qutayba ibn Muslim. Ibn Hajar described him as 'thiqa 'abid' (trustworthy ascetic) and al-Daraqutni as a trustworthy ascetic beset by weak narrators transmitting from him. Malik ibn Dinar counted him among the devoted 'readers of al-Rahman', and Basrans named him the finest man of their city.
research_evidence: Death year: Ibn Sa'd states 120 H, Ja'far ibn Sulayman says 123 H, Khalifa ibn Khayyat reports 127 H

bio: A Kufan judge and jurist of the Successors' generation who lived 72 years. Hammad ibn Zayd said he had not seen a more knowledgeable jurist from Kufa than Ibn Shubruma, and Sufyan al-Thawri characterized him as virtuous, strict, intelligent, trustworthy in hadith and eloquent.
research_teachers: Abu Zur'a ibn Amr ibn Jarir
research_evidence: مات سنة أربع وأربعين ومائة (died in the year 144 AH / 761 CE)

Ibn Hibban noted he was greatly prone to mistakes and confusion, and others said he sometimes confused chains and contradicted other narrators, though no outright fabricated texts were identified.

bio: Marwan served as secretary to Caliph Uthman and was badly wounded in the neck defending Uthman's house during the siege that ended in the caliph's assassination. He twice governed Medina under Mu'awiya and in 684 became the fourth Umayyad caliph, founding the Marwanid line that ruled until 750. Before his death he placed his son Abd al-Malik as successor and other sons in key governorships, entrenching hereditary succession.
research_evidence: After a reign of between six and ten months, depending on the source, Marwan died in the spring of 65 AH/685.

bio: A Medinan narrator described as trustworthy and abundant in hadith, who served as judge of Medina and was known as a storyteller of its people. His mother was Hind bint al-Muqawwam ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and his father Abu Amra (Bashir ibn Amr) was a companion. Sources differ on whether he himself was a young Companion or a Successor.
classif: storyteller (qass) of the people of Medina
research_students: Ishaq ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Talha

bio: Graded thiqa thabt (trustworthy and reliable) by al-Nasa'i and others. Sufyan ibn Uyayna considered him the most reliable of al-Zuhri's companions and knowledgeable of al-Zuhri's hadith. He was a close associate of Ibn Jurayj in Mecca before relocating to Yemen.

bio: A trustworthy senior Tabi'i of Basra, formerly enslaved and freed as an unconditional release (sa'iba). Known for asceticism, piety, and emphasis on following the Qur'an and Sunna without innovation. Scholars criticized one hadith of his about laughing during prayer, but held his other narrations sound and acceptable.
research_evidence: مات أبو العالية سنة ثلاث وتسعين (Abu al-Aliya died in the year 93 AH, per Ibn Manzur); alternate dates of 90, 106, 111, or 112 AH are also recorded

bio: A companion of the Prophet Muhammad who served as standard-bearer for the Ansar and later as governor of Egypt (656-657) under Ali. During a famine expedition he repeatedly slaughtered his own camels to feed starving troops. He resisted Mu'awiya's attempts to subvert his authority in Egypt and was undermined by forged letters falsely suggesting his defection.
research_evidence: He died in 59 AH (678–679 CE) during the final years of Mu'awiya's caliphate.
